pos: n. (proper name; father of Menahem king of Israel)
etymology: Hebrew Gadi, my fortune or Gadite, from gad, fortune, troop.
biblical_def: Gadi is known only as the father of a usurper: “For Menahem the son of Gadi went up from Tirzah, and came to Samaria, and smote Shallum the son of Jabesh in Samaria, and slew him, and reigned in his stead” (2 Kings 15:14). Shallum had reigned “a full month in Samaria” (2 Kings 15:13) after murdering Zachariah, the last of Jehu's line, and Menahem ended him in turn. The son of Gadi then smote Tiphsah because it would not open to him and ripped up its women with child, did evil all his days, and bought the favour of Pul king of Assyria with a thousand talents exacted from the mighty men of Israel. The northern kingdom's last decades are a succession of men known as the son of So-and-so, none of them the son of David, and Hosea's word fits them all: “They have set up kings, but not by me” (Hosea 8:4). Gadi's name may mean that he was a Gadite from beyond Jordan; it is remembered only because his son seized a throne.

In the nine and thirtieth year of Azariah king of Judah began Menahem the son of Gadi to reign over Israel, and reigned ten years in Samaria.
And Pul the king of Assyria came against the land: and Menahem gave Pul a thousand talents of silver, that his hand might be with him to confirm the kingdom in his hand.
Hos 8:4
They have set up kings, but not by me: they have made princes, and I knew it not: of their silver and their gold have they made them idols, that they may be cut off.
corruption_summary: Power seized is treated as power legitimated; Hosea calls the kings of Israel's last days kings set up without God.
corruption_paragraphs: Political realism holds that whoever holds power holds authority. The prophets of the northern kingdom refused that equation; the LORD ordains rulers, but He does not thereby approve every hand that grasps a crown.

The principle to recover is that legitimacy and providence are not the same. God permitted Menahem to reign and used Assyria to chasten Israel, and He also judged the son of Gadi for the blood by which he came to the throne.

pos: n. (proper name; father of Tibni, rival of Omri)
etymology: Hebrew Ginath, perhaps garden or protection, from ganan, to defend, or gan, garden.
biblical_def: Ginath is the father of Tibni, who contended with Omri for the throne of Israel: “Then were the people of Israel divided into two parts: half of the people followed Tibni the son of Ginath, to make him king; and half followed Omri” (1 Kings 16:21). The division came after Zimri's seven-day reign ended in fire at Tirzah, and for some years the northern kingdom had two claimants. The text closes the episode in a single sentence: “the people that followed Omri prevailed against the people that followed Tibni the son of Ginath: so Tibni died, and Omri reigned” (1 Kings 16:22). Omri went on to found Samaria and a dynasty whose son Ahab married Jezebel. Ginath's son lost, and lost quietly; Scripture does not say how he died. The episode is one of several in Kings where the people chose between men, and neither choice was the LORD's anointed.

corruption_summary: Popular choice is treated as divine sanction; the divided people of 1 Kings 16 chose between two men and got Ahab's dynasty.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern instinct is to equate the will of the majority with right. Half of Israel followed Tibni and half followed Omri, and the stronger half won; Scripture records it without praise for either.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a nation that has rejected the LORD's anointed may choose freely among its own and still choose ruin. Omri's victory opened the way to Ahab and Baal.

pos: n. (proper name; son of Hadad the Edomite, raised in Pharaoh's house)
biblical_def: Genubath is the son of Hadad the Edomite, the adversary the LORD stirred up against Solomon. Hadad had fled to Egypt as a child when Joab destroyed every male in Edom, and “found great favour in the sight of Pharaoh, so that he gave him to wife the sister of his own wife, the sister of Tahpenes the queen” (1 Kings 11:19). Of that marriage: “the sister of Tahpenes bare him Genubath his son, whom Tahpenes weaned in Pharaoh's house: and Genubath was in Pharaoh's household among the sons of Pharaoh” (1 Kings 11:20). The boy grew up a prince of Egypt and a kinsman of Edom's royal house, the living bond between two powers that had reason to resent Israel. When Hadad heard that David and Joab were dead he went home to trouble Solomon. The text says the LORD stirred him up, because Solomon's heart had turned to other gods. Genubath, named theft, is a reminder that the adversaries of the backslider are often raised quietly, in other men's houses, long before they appear.

corruption_paragraphs: The rise of Hadad and Rezon is easily explained in terms of a weakening empire. Kings does not deny the politics but names the cause above them: the LORD was angry with Solomon, because his heart was turned from the LORD God of Israel.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that providence uses secondary causes. An Edomite boy weaned in Pharaoh's house was being prepared, without knowing it, as a rod for a king who forsook the God of his father.

pos: n. (proper name; grandfather of Benhadad, founder of a Syrian dynasty)
biblical_def: Hezion is named once, in the genealogy of a Syrian king Asa hired against Israel: “king Asa sent them to Benhadad, the son of Tabrimon, the son of Hezion, king of Syria, that dwelt at Damascus” (1 Kings 15:18). Three generations of the royal house of Damascus are thus set down, and Hezion stands at its head. Many have identified him with Rezon, the adversary God raised against Solomon, who seized Damascus and reigned there, but the text does not say so, and the identification remains a conjecture. What the text does say is how Hezion's grandson came into Judah's history: Asa stripped the treasures of the LORD's house to buy a heathen king's alliance against his brethren in Israel, and Hanani the seer rebuked him for it, “Because thou hast relied on the king of Syria, and not relied on the LORD thy God” (2 Chronicles 16:7). The house of Hezion profited from Judah's unbelief.

corruption_summary: Alliances of convenience are counted as statesmanship; Hanani the seer counted Asa's Syrian league as a failure of faith.
corruption_paragraphs: Asa's purchase of Benhadad's help worked: Baasha withdrew and Ramah was dismantled. By the standards of statecraft it was a success. Hanani judged it by another standard and told the king that he had done foolishly.

The principle to recover is that means matter, not results alone. Cursed is the man that trusteth in man and maketh flesh his arm; a king who empties God's house to hire a heathen protector has already lost what the alliance was meant to save.

pos: n. (proper name; a daughter of Manasseh's house, mother of Abiezer)
etymology: Hebrew Hammoleketh, the queen or she who reigns, from malak, to reign, with the article.
biblical_def: Hammoleketh is a woman of the house of Manasseh: “And his sister Hammoleketh bare Ishod, and Abiezer, and Mahalah” (1 Chronicles 7:18). She was the sister of Gilead, the son of Machir, the son of Manasseh. Her name, the queen, is unusual for an Israelite woman and may preserve a title of honour. Her son Abiezer founded the clan of the Abiezrites, and that clan produced Gideon: the angel of the LORD “sat under an oak which was in Ophrah, that pertained unto Joash the Abiezrite” (Judges 6:11), and when the Spirit came upon Gideon, “he blew a trumpet; and Abiezer was gathered after him” (Judges 6:34). A woman named in one verse of a genealogy thus stands at the head of the family that delivered Israel from Midian. The Chronicler's practice of naming mothers in the lines of Manasseh is one of the ways Scripture honours the women through whom God built His people.

The principle to recover is that Scripture's order of the household does not diminish women. Headship in the line runs through fathers, and the record still honours the mother of a deliverer's house by name.

pos: n. (proper name; a daughter of the house of Etam in Judah)
etymology: Hebrew Hatselelponi, perhaps the shadow turns toward me, from tsel, shadow, and panah, to turn.
biblical_def: Hazelelponi is named in the genealogy of Judah as the sister of three brothers: “And these were of the father of Etam; Jezreel, and Ishma, and Idbash: and the name of their sister was Hazelelponi” (1 Chronicles 4:3). The verse belongs to the line of Hur, “the firstborn of Ephratah, the father of Bethlehem” (1 Chronicles 4:4), so she is a daughter of the Bethlehem clans from which David and, in the fullness of time, Christ would come. Her name is one of the longest in Scripture and its meaning is uncertain; a common reading is the shade turns toward me. That a sister should be named among brothers in a genealogy compiled chiefly by male descent marks her as notable in her generation, though nothing else is recorded. The Chronicler's first chapters are full of such names, preserved because every household of Judah mattered to the line through which the promise ran to Bethlehem.

pos: n. (proper name; a wife of Mered of Judah, sister of Naham)
etymology: Hebrew Hodiyyah, majesty of the LORD or splendour of Jah, from hod, majesty, and Yah, the LORD.
biblical_def: Hodiah is named in the genealogy of Judah: “And the sons of his wife Hodiah the sister of Naham, the father of Keilah the Garmite, and Eshtemoa the Maachathite” (1 Chronicles 4:19). The King James margin notes that she is the woman called Jehudijah in the verse before: “And his wife Jehudijah bare Jered the father of Gedor, and Heber the father of Socho, and Jekuthiel the father of Zanoah. And these are the sons of Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, which Mered took” (1 Chronicles 4:18). Jehudijah means the Jewess, and the name seems to distinguish her, the Judahite wife of Mered, from his Egyptian wife Bithiah, the daughter of Pharaoh. Hodiah's sons founded the towns of Keilah and Eshtemoa in the hill country of Judah. The same name, spelled Hodijah, belongs to Levites in Nehemiah who led the people in confession. Here it marks a mother of towns in Judah, set beside an Egyptian princess in a household that joined Israel.

The Chronicler marks the distinction carefully, calling one wife the Jewess and the other the daughter of Pharaoh, while counting the sons of both in Judah.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the covenant people were defined by covenant, not blood alone. A daughter of Pharaoh could be numbered in Judah, as Rahab and Ruth were, when she joined herself to the God of Israel.

pos: n. (proper name; a wife of Shaharaim the Benjamite)
etymology: Hebrew Chodesh, new moon or month, from chadash, to be new, to renew.
biblical_def: Hodesh is a wife of Shaharaim, a Benjamite who lived for a time in Moab: “And Shaharaim begat children in the country of Moab, after he had sent them away; Hushim and Baara were his wives. And he begat of Hodesh his wife, Jobab, and Zibia, and Mesha, and Malcham” (1 Chronicles 8:8-9). The verse is terse and troubling. Shaharaim sent away two wives and took another in Moab, and his sons by her became “heads of the fathers” (1 Chronicles 8:10). Several of their names, Mesha and Malcham, sound Moabite or Ammonite, as if the family had taken on the colour of the land. The Chronicler records it without comment, but the record itself teaches. Elimelech's sojourn in Moab cost him his sons; Shaharaim's left a household with Moabite names in the genealogy of Benjamin. Hodesh's name means new moon, a word Israel knew from its feasts.

The principle to recover is that marriage is a covenant, not an arrangement of convenience, and that sojourning among the nations carries danger to a household's faith. Shaharaim's sons by Hodesh bore Moab's names into Benjamin's roll.

pos: n. (proper name; a wife of Ashur, the father of Tekoa)
etymology: Hebrew Chel'ah, rust or scum, from chel'ah, the rust of a pot.
biblical_def: Helah is one of the two wives of Ashur of Judah: “And Ashur the father of Tekoa had two wives, Helah and Naarah” (1 Chronicles 4:5). Of her children the Chronicler writes, “And the sons of Helah were, Zereth, and Jezoar, and Ethnan” (1 Chronicles 4:7). Ashur is called the father of Tekoa, that is, the founder or chief of the town in Judah's hill country that later produced the wise woman who pleaded for Absalom and the herdman-prophet Amos. Helah's name is strange to modern ears: the Hebrew word means the rust or scum of a pot, the very word Ezekiel uses of Jerusalem's uncleansed filth. Whatever lay behind the naming, Scripture records her as a mother of Judah's households, and her sons are counted with the rest. A name of reproach was no bar to a place in the line.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God gives a new name to those He saves. The rust Ezekiel saw in the pot of Jerusalem is purged by fire and by grace, not by a better word on the birth record.

pos: n. (proper name; a Danite, grandfather of the blasphemer stoned in the wilderness)
etymology: Hebrew Dibri, eloquent or my word, from dabar, to speak.
biblical_def: Dibri is named in the account of the first recorded blasphemer in Israel: “And the Israelitish woman's son blasphemed the name of the LORD, and cursed. And they brought him unto Moses: (and his mother's name was Shelomith, the daughter of Dibri, of the tribe of Dan:)” (Leviticus 24:11). The young man was the son of an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father, and he strove with a man of Israel in the camp. Moses put him in ward until the LORD should shew His mind, and the answer became a statute: “he that blasphemeth the name of the LORD, he shall surely be put to death, and all the congregation shall certainly stone him: as well the stranger, as he that is born in the land” (Leviticus 24:16). Dibri's name is a bitter irony; it is built on the Hebrew word for speaking, and his grandson's sin was a sin of the mouth. Scripture names the mother's father and tribe so that the judgment fell on a known man, not an anonymous stranger.

corruption_summary: Blasphemy is treated as a harmless expression of opinion; the law treated it as a capital offence against the holy name.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern law and culture regard blasphemy as at worst a discourtesy. Leviticus 24 treats the cursing of the Name as among the gravest crimes in Israel, judged by God's own direct word and applied to stranger and native alike.

The principle to recover is the holiness of God's name. The civil penalty belonged to Israel's theocracy, but the moral law stands: the LORD will not hold him guiltless that taketh His name in vain, and the third commandment binds every tongue.
